Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 6:49pm

By Caitlin Rawling

Thank you for joining us. This is where we will end our live coverage for the day.

Here are the key developments from today:

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 6:36pm

By Caitlin Rawling

Israel's defence minister says that Israeli forces will remain in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza indefinitely, hours after the United States and Iran agreed to end the Middle East war, including in Lebanon.

"Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and I are pursuing a clear policy under which the IDF will remain in the security zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza for an unlimited period of time, in order to protect the border and Israeli communities from there against jihadist elements," Israel Katz said in a statement.

Reporting by AFP

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 6:13pm

By Caitlin Rawling

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi has said Israeli attacks in Lebanon must be completely halted, and the US bears responsibility for implementing the framework deal on ending the war.

Araqchi said this to his Turkish, Iraqi and Egyptian counterparts today in separate calls, according to his Telegram account.

Reporting by Reuters

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:42pm

By Caitlin Rawling

The United States and Iran are to hold indirect meetings in Doha this week ahead of the formal signing of a deal aimed at ending the Middle East war, a diplomat has told AFP.

"Separate preparatory meetings with each side will now take place in Doha this week ahead of the official signing in Switzerland and the start of the technical talks," the diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive arrangements.

The source added that Qatari mediators had departed Tehran after "17 hours of intensive negotiations", which began on Sunday and culminated in an agreement.

Reporting by AFP

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 5:17pm

By Caitlin Rawling

It's five long days between now and the proposed time for signing a deal between the United States and Iran which, from what we know at the moment, falls somewhere between a ceasefire and a peace deal.

You can read more in Laura Tingle's analysis here:

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:50pm

By Caitlin Rawling

Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, has denounced the deal between the United States and Iran to end the Middle East war, including in Lebanon, insisting his country is not bound by it.

"Trump's agreement does not bind us … we are not party to this agreement. It does not safeguard our security," Ben Gvir said on his Telegram channel in the first reaction from an Israeli official to the deal.

"We must not settle for anything less than the dismantling of Hezbollah.

"We must not withdraw from a single inch of territory that our soldiers have captured and cleared of terrorist infrastructure."

Reporting by AFP

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:33pm

By Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran

As Donald Trump was trying to push his Iran deal over the line, Benjamin Netanyahu bombed Beirut, showing once again the Israeli prime minister has other priorities.

You can read more here:

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 4:09pm

By Caitlin Rawling

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has welcomed the ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran.

"The priority now is its swift and full implementation by all parties," von der Leyen said in a post on X.

"This agreement should allow for the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

"It opens the door to broader negotiations on peace and security in the Middle East.

"And should end Iran's nuclear and ballistic programmes and its destabilising activities in the region.

"And of course there can be no peace in the Middle East while Lebanon is in flames.

"Once again Europe calls on all parties to respect Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity and implement a genuine ceasefire," she said in the post.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 3:37pm

By Brianna Morris- Grant

Photos taken today from Musandam in Oman show vessels dotting the Strait of Hormuz.

The Musandam Peninsula juts out into the strait, giving it its distinct curved shape.

Prior to the blockade, more than 100 commercial ships passed through the strait every day.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 3:18pm

By Stephen Letts

The ceasefire deal and hopes that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen is dominating global markets today and is driving down oil prices.

But there are still a lot of questions about whether oil (or about 20 per cent of the global supply that has been locked in) will really start to flow again, when fuel supplies will normalise and what's next for oil prices?

Carrington Clarke and our roving finance guru Alan Kohler give these questions and plenty more a decent thrashing in the latest edition of our Fuelcast podast.

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 3:00pm

By Courtney Gould

So with the end of the war in sight, what does that do to the government's thinking about extending the fuel excise cut?

The fuel excise was halved in April to tackle high prices as a result of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says, with the ceasefire agreement only just announced, the government will continue to monitor the issue, with a decision to be made in the coming days.

"We'll make an assessment over the coming period and we'll make an appropriate announcement. We know that the end of the conflict doesn't mean that we're back to business as usual. And we know that that has been really important in providing support for people," he says.

Albanese also notes the first round of tax cuts passed last year will come into effect on July 1, the same day the fuel excise is due to return to its normal rate.

The PM says the expenditure review committee is due to meet next week.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:35pm

By Asia Editor Karishma Vyas

Recent unrest over the US deal is posing a major challenge for the regime and signals a rift in the top leadership between hardliners, advocating for a full-blown assault on Israel and US interests in the Middle East, and more moderate factions which are pushing to end the conflict and focus on the grave economic conditions afflicting the country.

Iran's President, Masoud Pezeshkian, rebuffed the demands of some protestors by saying: "The Supreme National Security Council has decisively approved that we should negotiate."

It is important to note that Iran is in the grip of it's worst economic crisis, with inflation at about 70 per cent and the value of the currency in freefall.

The public discontent erupted into mass protests in December and January, with thousands of ordinary citizens taking to the streets to demand economic relief from the government.

What started as a strike by merchants in Tehran's Grand Bazaar over the plummeting value of the rial against the dollar quickly escalated to widespread anger directed at the regime.

To quell the largest protests the country had seen since the 1979 revolution, security forces unleashed a deadly crackdown that killed at least 6,400 people in a matter of days, according to US-based human rights group HRANA. The UN estimates the real dead toll could be much higher.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi announced that the new deal with the US would be signed on Friday in Switzerland, according to Tasnim News.

All eyes will be on Iran this week to see how people react to news of this US deal and what exactly the regime chooses to do about it.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:18pm

By Asia Editor Karishma Vyas

Addressing a domestic audience, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi has portrayed the peace deal as a major victory for the regime.

"The enemy that had launched an attack to carry out its sinister objectives suffered defeat in all its goals, and the Islamic Republic of Iran achieved great victories in the war," he is quoted as saying by Iranian media.

"The memorandum of understanding was not just a product of diplomacy, but is indebted to Iran's military achievements. It is indebted to the pure blood of the martyrs we gave in confronting the enemies of the establishment," he said.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 2:02pm

By Asia Editor Karishma Vyas

It's just after 7am in Iran's capital Tehran and people are waking up to news that a ceasefire deal has been struck, but before this deal was announced there was some unhappiness at the prospect of peace.

Wide-scale protests were held across the capital Tehran and other cities by hardline supporters of the regime opposing any agreement.

Video shared online by Saberin News showed crowds of men and women dressed in the traditional black chador marching in the streets, demanding the resignation of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, both of whom are key negotiators with the US.

Demonstrators were seen outside the foreign ministry office chanting "Death to Araghchi, the shameless compromiser" and "Death to Araghchi, the shameless infiltrator."

"Araghchi, Qalibaf, what about my leader's blood?" some demonstrators shouted in reference to the killing of then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in an Israeli airstrike.

In some cities, protestors burned photos of the two senior political figures, along with images of US President Donald Trump and Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

While this conservative and deeply religious faction of Iranian society is the most vocal in the country, most Iranians are not supportive of escalating the conflict.

It remains to be seen how people will react to news of this ceasefire deal, which was confirmed in the early hours of Monday morning in Iran.

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:48pm

By Joshua Boscaini

The opposition leader has welcomed the ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran, but says the opposition wants to see the details.

In a statement, Angus Taylor says the agreement must be lasting, durable, enforceable and backed by action to keep the Strait of Hormuz open.

The Coalition says it's "deeply disappointing" the prime minister wasn't able to secure an invitation to this year's G7 Leaders Summit in France.

"At a time when decisions are being made that will affect Australian fuel prices, energy security and regional stability Australia should be at the table," Taylor says.

"The Coalition supports serious efforts to de-escalate the conflict, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore stability in the Middle East.

"Australia must stand with our partners, defend freedom of navigation and protect Australians from the worst impacts of global instability."

You can read more here in our federal politics blog:

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:29pm

By Annika Burgess

While welcoming the deal, US Republican Senator Lindsay Graham also expressed concern about conflicting statements regarding its details.

"I will be watching closely the ensuing negotiations regarding Iran's nuclear program and other matters," he wrote on X.

"I am somewhat concerned that Iran's view of the agreement seems different than what the American negotiating team is claiming."

The only details about what's in Tehran's draft agreement have been trickling out through Iranian state media and have not been verified.

A report published on Friday by Mehr News — an outlet linked to the Iranian government — purported to show a draft of Iran's 14-point ceasefire plan, which suggested it was getting a lot of the things it was hoping for.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 1:04pm

By Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran

The alliance between the Israeli prime minister and the United States president has been tested over the weekend after Israel attacked a claimed Hezbollah command centre in the southern suburbs of Beirut, which Donald Trump says was an overreaction.

Israeli TV network Channel 12 reported the prime minister's team viewed Trump's admonishment as a "slap in the face".

Over the weekend, Israeli media had been reporting the rumblings within the Netanyahu government and the Israeli military establishment about the prospect of a peace deal between the US and Iran.

Netanyahu had been largely sidelined during the negotiations, learning about the progress of talks rather than being intimately involved in them.

The reports suggested there was deep frustration that the US was entertaining a deal, and a view that pursuing an agreement legitimised the Tehran regime's tactics during the war.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 12:37pm

By Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is yet to comment on the ceasefire between the US and Iran, but he did make sure to wish Donald Trump a happy birthday on social media.

"Happy birthday Mr President," Netanyahu said in a post on X.

"America celebrates 250 years of freedom — a great nation built on liberty and faith.

"I wish you continued strength and vigour as you lead America towards a bright future of peace through strength, and as we continue to bring the US-Israel alliance to ever greater heights," Netanyahu said in the post.

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 12:16pm

By Stephen Letts

News of a US-Iran ceasefire agreement and the likely reopening of the Strait of Hormuz has put a rocket under Asian share markets.

At 10:50am AEST, Japan's Nikkei had gained 4.6% and South Korea's Kospi was up 5.6%.

The ASX 200 is up 1.5%.

Key Event

Mon 15 Jun 2026 at 12:01pm

By Annika Burgess

US Vice-President JD Vance said the agreement with Iran had the potential to "fundamentally transform the Middle East for the next 50 years".

If Iran complied with the deal, he said the agreement would ensure Tehran "will never have a nuclear weapon", including by preventing Iran from "pursuing, procuring or trying to buy one".

Speaking to Fox News, Mr Vance also claimed the deal could lead to "a new era of Middle East prosperity".

"It's going to make the Middle East more investable," he said.

If it was a region the US didn't have to "worry about so much", Mr Vance said, "we can generate a lot of prosperity for the American people out of that region."
